props.title: Belle de Jour
props.initialSlug: Elegant wife leads secret life as daytime prostitute

sections.content: Belle de Jour (1967) stands as Luis Buñuel's masterful exploration of bourgeois sexuality and repression. Catherine Deneuve delivers a career-defining performance as Séverine, a wealthy housewife who secretly works at a brothel while her husband is at work. The film's genius lies in how it blends reality with fantasy - Buñuel never clearly delineates between Séverine's daydreams and actual events. This influenced later psychological dramas like Mulholland Drive (2001) and Eyes Wide Shut (1999), which similarly blur the lines between sexual fantasy and reality.

sections.content: Buñuel's trademark surrealism reaches new heights in how he portrays Séverine's sexual awakening. The film's opening carriage scene immediately establishes its dreamlike quality, while later sequences in the brothel maintain an air of artificiality that questions everything we're seeing. This approach influenced contemporary filmmakers like David Lynch, particularly in Blue Velvet (1986) and Lost Highway (1997), which similarly explore the dark underbelly of seemingly perfect relationships.

The film's examination of class structure and sexual politics remains startlingly relevant. Like The Piano Teacher (2001) and Secretary (2002), it presents female sexuality as complex and potentially destructive, while questioning society's madonna-whore complex. Deneuve's porcelain beauty and controlled performance create an fascinating tension between appearance and desire. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: The influence of Belle de Jour resonates through contemporary cinema, particularly in films exploring female sexuality and desire. Under the Skin (2013) and The Handmaiden (2016) echo its themes of sexual awakening and power dynamics, while maintaining similarly dreamlike atmospheres. The way Buñuel handles Séverine's inner life - through subtle gestures and loaded glances rather than explicit exposition - created a template for character studies like Carol (2015) and Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019).
